newsitem.title: USA: U.S. pork industry may spend more on market access.
newsitem.headline: U.S. pork industry may spend more on market access.

text.p: U.S. pork producers, riding the wave of booming exports, may dip into their own bulging surplus funds to promote market access abroad for U.S. pork, because planned 1997 government funding won't increase.
"That will have to be addressed," Carnell Korsmeyer, president of the National Pork Board, told Reuters at the National Pork Producers Council meeting here.
"That's probably one of the things that will be considered for the surplus. But that's not been determined," she said.

The U.S. Agriculture Department said earlier on Thursday that it allocated $90 million to 64 trade groups for export promotion and market access, unchanged from 1996. The U.S. Meat Export Federation will get $8.5 million.

Pork exports in 1996 hit a record $915 million, up 19 percent from a year earlier, with another large rise projected for this year by the USDA due in part to expected trade liberalization with countries such as South Korea and Japan.

The Pork Board is an industry group that adminsters "checkoff" funds, a 45-cent share for every $100 of pork sold every year. The funds are used for advertising, consumer education, and other pork industry promotion.
The board may have a budget surplus of as much as $10 million this year in surplus funds, Korsmeyer said.

The board's budget for calendar 1997 of $58.4 million included a projected surplus this year of $2.2 million. But the group also has a carryover surplus from last year of $6 million and larger than expected pork sales in 1997 could make the total surplus even higher.
"It's actually projected to be around $10 million," she said.
